To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
“A simple ensemble of ridge regression models trained in various sub–spaces of chemical space, selected iteratively, can be a competitive method for predicting toxicity of chemicals”.
a simple ridge regression ensemble trained on a subset of the chemical space can outperform more sophisticated models.
the ridge regression ensemble outperforms the best individual ridge regression model, and that the ensemble of ridge regression models outperforms the ensemble of random forest models.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new, purely data–driving approach to QSAR modeling of chemical toxicity, based on ensemble regression models, trained on various subspaces of chemical space.

the following issues: • development of an efficient data–driven model for toxicity prediction; • development of a method of selecting the most relevant chemical features, which is based on a novel iterative procedure; • development of an algorithm of selecting the most appropriate chemical subspaces, in which individual models should be trained; • evaluation of the proposed model within a real–life application, namely, the Environmental Toxicity prediction Challenge CADASTER 09.
the following questions: (a) Can a purely data–based approach to QSAR model building be competitive with the state–of–the–art?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presented method is a competitive approach for the prediction of chemical toxicity.
our approach was among the most competitive ones in the challenge, and it has the potential to become one of the most accurate and robust approaches for predicting toxicity in the future.
the presented approach can compete with the best methods developed for this challenge.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
our approach was able to predict the toxicity of compounds with a similar accuracy as the best method of the competition, without using any domain–specific knowledge.
we were able to obtain a very competitive result in a challenging problem, using a simple, purely data–driving approach.
the approach proposed in the paper is competitive with the best performing methods of the challenge and can be successfully employed for toxicity prediction.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the absence of domain knowledge, it is possible to achieve results competitive with state–of–the–art methods by using a relatively simple and generic approach.
the presented approach is able to achieve a high level of accuracy, even when trained on data from a single chemical family.
a purely data–based approach to QSAR modeling is possible, and may yield competitive performance.
